pages.scope: Cellar spiders (family Pholcidae) for US and Canadian readers: the spider most people mean by "daddy long legs" indoors, identification and the bite question first. The quick answer: a tiny pale body on very long, thin legs, hanging upside down in a loose web in a basement, crawl space, garage or ceiling corner, that vibrates in its web until it blurs when disturbed, and that is not known to bite people (Penn State; UMN). Sizes only from sources (Penn State's long-bodied cellar spider: body about 1/4 to 5/16 inch, a female's front legs about 2 inches). The species people meet, each only as a source covers it: the long-bodied cellar spider, the most common of its family in the US (Penn State), the marbled cellar spider, which has displaced it in California (UC IPM), and the short-bodied cellar spider. "Cellar spider bite" and "are daddy long legs poisonous" answered at the sources' strength: Penn State says cellar spiders are not known to bite people; the story that they are the most venomous spider but cannot bite has no scientific basis, and harvestmen have no venom glands or fangs (UC Riverside's daddy-long-legs page; Missouri Dept. of Conservation); never a bite photo, never a diagnosis (bites in general: /blog/what-does-a-spider-bite-look-like). "Cellar spider vs harvestman" gets its own h2 and the quick-ID table (traits as rows: body parts, eyes, silk and web, legs, where you find it, venom), from the sources: a harvestman has one oval body with no waist, two eyes and no silk (MDC), a cellar spider two body parts, a cluster of eyes and a messy web (Penn State, MDC). The third "daddy longlegs", the crane fly, gets one card and one line that link /blog/mosquito-hawk-explained, which keeps every crane fly search. Then the female carrying her eggs in her jaws (one line; /blog/spider-egg-sacs), what cellar spiders eat (only as a source says; answer "do daddy long legs eat silverfish" only if one does), why they live indoors all year, and what to do: leave them, or remove webs with a broom or vacuum (UMN); control goes to /blog/how-to-get-rid-of-spiders (planned) or /blog/house-spiders. Cards: harvestman, crane fly, common house spider (/blog/house-spiders), brown recluse ("cellar spider vs brown recluse" stays with /blog/brown-recluse-look-alikes: one line and a link), camel cricket (/blog/camel-crickets, the long-legged basement jumper called a spider cricket). Link /tools/spider-identifier as the next step. Sources: Penn State Extension (long-bodied cellar spider), UMN Extension, UC IPM, UC Riverside (Vetter), Missouri Dept. of Conservation, as already cited on /blog/house-spiders, /blog/venomous-spiders, /blog/spiders-in-california and /tools/spider-identifier. No pesticide advice; no quote prompt (a traffic page).

Needed, none on record: a cellar spider in its web in a basement, garage or ceiling corner (where people find it; the formula wants two such shots), a marbled cellar spider (Holocnemus pluchei) for western readers, a short-bodied cellar spider (Spermophora senoculata), a harvestman in place (wall, siding, plant or tree trunk) and a group of harvestmen, ideally a cellar spider and a harvestman at the same scale. pages.scope: Trichonephila clavata, the East Asian orb weaver spreading across the Southeast, for US readers. The quick answer: how to recognize a female (large, with a yellow and blue-black banded body, long black-and-yellow banded legs and a big golden web, often several webs together) and the much smaller brown male; that bites are rare and not considered medically important, at the sources' strength; where it has been recorded so far (states only as a dated source lists them; first reported in northeast Georgia, per the University of Georgia), and how it spreads (young spiders balloon on silk; hitchhiking on vehicles, as sources say; "flying joro spiders" answered as ballooning, never as flight). Joro or a native look-alike: the golden silk orb weaver ("banana spider"), the yellow garden spider and the banded garden spider, in a quick-ID table under the quick answer (size, abdomen pattern, legs, web, season, range) and look-alike cards linking orb-weaver-spiders (same release) and /blog/spiders-in-florida for the golden silk orb weaver. Season (webs most noticeable in late summer and fall; what happens with frost, as sources say) and what researchers say about effects on native species and on cold tolerance, at their strength. What to do: the sources' advice on leaving or removing webs; no spray advice; report sightings only where a state program asks for reports (name and link the program). A state list with its date, or a map only if the writer can build it from cited, dated state-level records (a GuideMap from data/geo). Sources: University of Georgia (Odum School of Ecology and UGA Extension), Clemson HGIC, NC State Extension, other state extension or natural history programs that publish records, and peer-reviewed range papers cited only as their abstracts say. No quote prompt.

pages.scope: Re-aimed to the searcher's words, "carpet beetle bites". The answer first: carpet beetles do not bite; the itchy, bite-like bumps some people get are a reaction to the larvae's hairs (carpet beetle dermatitis), as Penn State Extension, Texas A&M AgriLife and the CDC's Emerging Infectious Diseases report say, and most people never react (at the sources' strength). A quick-ID table under the quick answer: carpet beetle rash vs bed bug bites vs flea bites vs scabies vs mosquito bites: what it looks like, where on the body, when it appears, the sign to look for, each cell from a source (CDC, AAD or a medical school for the bites). What the rash looks like (red, itchy bumps or welts, often under clothing or where skin touched bedding or upholstery; never diagnose), who reacts (an acquired allergy, as Penn State says), how to confirm it (find the larvae and their cast skins: link /blog/signs-of-carpet-beetles and /blog/carpet-beetle-larvae), relief at the sources' strength (wash, launder bedding, an over-the-counter anti-itch cream only if a medical source names it), when to see a doctor (spreading or infected skin, eye or breathing symptoms, or no larvae found: scabies and other causes need a clinician), and the fix in one short section linking /blog/how-to-get-rid-of-carpet-beetles. Cards: carpet beetle larva (/blog/carpet-beetle-larvae), bites but no bed bugs (/blog/bed-bug-bites-but-no-bed-bugs), bed bug bites and flea bites (no link until the US pages are live), scabies (no link). Never write that carpet beetles bite, burrow into skin or live on people. Sources: Penn State Extension (Carpet Beetle Dermatitis), CDC EID 2021 (Anthrenus dermatitis cluster), Texas A&M AgriLife, UC IPM, University of Kentucky, AAD or a medical school for bite care. No quote prompt.

pages.scope: Camel crickets for US and Canadian readers, identification first: a humpbacked, wingless cricket, light tan to dark brown, with antennae much longer than its body and large hind legs, that never chirps (no sound-making organs, per Clemson HGIC; chirping indoors points to field crickets, per NC State) and jumps a surprisingly long way (MDC); sizes only from sources (Clemson: 1/2 to 1 1/2 inches; MDC: body up to about 1 inch). The "jumps at you" reputation only as a source puts it: NC State, Clemson and MDC do not say they jump toward people, and it is never an attack. Which ones get into homes: the greenhouse camel cricket (Tachycines asynamorus, also written Diestrammena asynamora), the most common camel cricket in eastern US homes (Epps et al. 2014, PeerJ; NC State), and the native camel or cave crickets (Ceuthophilus); nymphs look like small adults (NC State). Then the "spider cricket" question, spider or cricket (six legs and long antennae against a spider's eight legs and none), with look-alike cards: house and field cricket (crickets-in-house, once live), cellar spider (/blog/house-spiders), wolf spider (/blog/wolf-spiders), house centipede (/blog/house-centipedes). Where they live and why they come in: damp basements, crawl spaces, garages and laundry rooms; outdoors under stones, logs, firewood, mulch and ivy; large numbers point to a moisture problem (MDC); whether they breed indoors, where sources differ (MDC and Iowa State: unlikely unless it stays dark and damp; Cornell's Nassau County office: they can). Bites and harm at the sources' strength: none of the sources read reports a bite (MDC and Kentucky call them harmless); damage only as Clemson (fine fabrics and houseplants when numerous) and NC State (stored garments and linens after a long infestation; dark fecal smears on joists) put it. A control section, since this page owns "how to get rid of camel crickets": dry the space, seal and weather-strip, pull mulch, firewood and stored boxes back from walls, sticky traps in corners and behind appliances, vacuum (NC State, Clemson); insecticides only as those sources put them (perimeter first, baits in crawl spaces, a product labeled for the site; the label is the law), no product names. One line each, linked once live: chirping crickets (crickets-in-house) and the unrelated desert camel spider (camel-spiders); the western Jerusalem cricket is another family (UC IPM), one line at most. Sources: NC State Extension's Camel Crickets (revised 2023), Clemson HGIC, University of Maryland Extension, University of Kentucky, MDC, Iowa State, Epps et al. 2014.

pages.scope: The big web builders of late summer and fall, for US and Canadian readers, identification first. The quick answer: an orb weaver builds the classic round, wheel-shaped web, and the ones people notice are large females from late summer into fall; bites are rare and not considered dangerous, at the sources' strength. The species, each with a photo where the ledger has one: the yellow garden spider (Argiope aurantia, the zigzag band in the web; "writing spider" only if a source uses the name), the banded garden spider, the cross orb weaver (Araneus diadematus), marbled and barn orb weavers, the golden silk orb weaver (Trichonephila clavipes, called "banana spider" in the Southeast; one line that the name is also used for the huntsman, as /blog/spiders-in-florida already says), the spinybacked orb weaver (Gasteracantha cancriformis) and, in a short section with a card that links joro-spiders, the Joro spider. "Banana spider" is a side target here; "banana spider florida" stays with /blog/spiders-in-florida. Webs and season: why they appear by doors, porch lights and gardens late in the season, how often webs are rebuilt, egg sacs in fall (link /blog/spider-egg-sacs) and what happens over winter, each as sources say. Bites and "are orb weavers poisonous", at the sources' strength, linking /blog/what-does-a-spider-bite-look-like (frozen until Oct 30: link only). A quick-ID table under the quick answer, one row per species: size, color and markings, web, where and when found, range by region from the sources. pages.scope: Jumping spiders (family Salticidae) for US and Canadian readers who find a small, fuzzy, big-eyed spider that hops on a windowsill, wall, deck rail or car mirror; identification first. The quick answer: what makes a jumping spider (two very large forward-facing eyes, a compact hairy body and short legs; it hunts by sight and pounces instead of waiting in a catching web), sizes only from sources, and that bites are uncommon and minor, at the sources' strength (a bite can happen when one is pressed or handled; none of the common species is treated as medically important by the extension sources). The species people meet, each with a photo where the ledger has one: the bold jumping spider (Phidippus audax: black with a white or orange spot pattern and iridescent green or blue jaws), Johnson's jumping spider (red abdomen, mainly in the West), the zebra jumping spider (Salticus scenicus, black-and-white striped, on house walls) and others only where a source and a photo exist; patterns vary within a species (Colorado State). Where and when they turn up indoors (sunny windows; they wander in and do not infest a house), what they eat (other insects, as sources say), and babies: spiderlings look like small adults; the silk retreat and egg sac only as sources describe them, linking /blog/spider-egg-sacs. The bite section: what a bite is like and when to get care, from CDC/NIOSH or extension pages, never diagnosing a wound as a spider bite, linking /blog/what-does-a-spider-bite-look-like (frozen until Oct 30: link only). A quick-ID table under the quick answer: jumping spider and its look-alikes (wolf spider, black widow, false widow, parson spider, ant-mimic jumping spiders): size, eyes, body, web or no web, where found, bite. Cards: black spiders (/blog/black-spiders), wolf spider (/blog/wolf-spiders), black widow (black-widow-spiders, no link until live), house spiders (/blog/house-spiders). What to do: leave it or move it outside with a cup and a card; no spray advice (spider control belongs to how-to-get-rid-of-spiders, linked once live). The pet-keeping searches (for sale, enclosure, care) are not targeted: one line at most. Sources: Colorado State Extension, Penn State Extension, UC IPM (spiders), Washington State University Bug Info, Missouri Department of Conservation, University of Kentucky, Texas A&M AgriLife, whichever cover the species shown. No product advice beyond the one generic pick; no quote prompt (a traffic page).

pages.scope: Yellow sac spiders (Cheiracanthium) for US and Canadian readers, and for the reader who searched "white house spider" or "sac spider": a small, pale yellow to cream spider, sometimes greenish, with darker jaws and foot tips (Penn State), about 1/5 to 2/5 inch (UMN; Penn State gives females as 3/16 to 3/8 inch), that hunts at night on walls and ceilings without a web and hides by day in a flat silk sac in a wall-ceiling corner or behind shelves and pictures, dropping to the floor when disturbed (UC IPM). The quick answer bolds the tell: a pale spider that spends the day inside a small silk sac in a corner. The two common species, the agrarian (American) yellow sac spider and the longlegged (northern) yellow sac spider, which Penn State says is found mostly in buildings and lays its eggs almost exclusively indoors; where each lives in the US and Canada only as sources give it. A pale-spider sorter for the "white house spider" search (no source uses it as a species name): a quick-ID table, one row per pale spider people find indoors (yellow sac spider; cellar spider, linking /blog/daddy-long-legs; others only where a source supports them, for example a freshly molted spider or a white crab spider carried in on flowers), with size, color, web or sac, where you find it and the tell. Bites at the evidence's strength: Penn State says the two common sac spiders account for a significant number of bites, usually when one is trapped against skin in bedding, clothing or shoes, painful and burning at first with redness and swelling, normally without serious medical problems; studies of verified bites did not find the dying-tissue wounds once blamed on them (Vetter and colleagues' 20 verified bites, as /blog/venomous-spiders cites them); when to see a doctor only at a medical source's strength (CDC or a state health department); never diagnose from a photo (link /blog/what-does-a-spider-bite-look-like and /tools/bug-bite-identifier). "Yellow sac spider vs brown recluse" stays with /blog/brown-recluse-look-alikes: a two-sentence section and a link. Then when they come indoors (the season only as a source gives it), the retreat and egg sac (/blog/spider-egg-sacs), and what to do: shake out clothes and shoes, vacuum the silk sacs, seal gaps (sources only); control goes to /blog/how-to-get-rid-of-spiders (planned). Cards: cellar spider, brown recluse, common house spider (/blog/house-spiders, which keeps "house spider"), false widow. Link /tools/spider-identifier as the next step. Sources: Penn State Extension (agrarian and longlegged sac spiders), UC IPM, UMN Extension, the verified-bite study, CDC or a state health department for care. No pesticide advice; no quote prompt (a traffic page).

pages.scope: Solifuges (order Solifugae), called camel spiders, sun spiders and wind scorpions, for US readers, the desert Southwest and West first. The quick answer: an arachnid but not a true spider (no silk for webs, huge forward jaws, what look like ten legs because the leg-like pedipalps sit in front), fast and mostly nocturnal, and harmless to people apart from a painful pinch if handled; whether they have venom only as sources say. Size and speed, separated from the myths (the wartime "giant camel spider" photos, claims that they scream, chase people or eat camels), each myth answered only as a named source debunks it. Where they live in the US (arid Southwest and West, as range sources give it) and why one turns up on a porch or in a garage at night (drawn to lights and the insects around them, as sources say). The bite: what it does and when to get care, at the sources' strength. A quick-ID table under the quick answer: camel spider and its look-alikes (wolf spider, tarantula, scorpion, whip scorpion): body shape, jaws, legs, speed, where found, bite or sting. Cards: wolf spider (/blog/wolf-spiders), tarantula (tarantulas, no link until live), scorpion (scorpions, no link until live), camel cricket (/blog/camel-crickets: the name only). What to do: sweep one into a container and release it outside; no spray advice. Sources: Texas A&M AgriLife, University of Arizona Cooperative Extension, UC Riverside or UC IPM, the Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum, the Smithsonian or the American Museum of Natural History where they cover solifuges, and peer-reviewed work cited only as its abstract says. No quote prompt.

pages.scope: US edition, identification first: the adult drain fly (moth fly or sewer fly; family Psychodidae, the common bathroom species Clogmia albipunctata) and its larvae (the "small black worms in the bathroom" that live in the slimy film inside drains), with photos at a printed scale. Where they breed: the organic film (biofilm) in sink, tub, shower and floor drains, overflow holes, garbage disposals and sump pits, and hidden sources (a broken drain line under a slab, a dry trap, a leaking toilet seal), as sources list them. Find the source first: the tape test (clear tape over each drain overnight) and checking overflows. The fix, in order: scrub the film out with a long stiff brush, an enzyme or bacterial drain cleaner where sources recommend one, keep traps filled with water, repair leaks and broken lines; why boiling water, bleach and foggers do little on their own (at the sources' strength); insecticides only as extension sources put them (sprays for adults do not reach the source; the label is the law). "Gnats in drain" answered here. Drain fly or another small fly: a quick-ID table under the quick answer (drain fly, fruit fly, fungus gnat, phorid fly): wings and body shape, how it flies, where it breeds, the fix; link fruit-flies (mustLink, same release), /blog/how-to-get-rid-of-gnats and /learn/how-to-get-rid-of-fungus-gnats. Are they harmful: a nuisance, at the sources' strength. Cards: fruit fly (fruit-flies), fungus gnat (/learn/how-to-get-rid-of-fungus-gnats), phorid fly and other gnats (/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-gnats), small moths (/blog/moths-in-house). Regional pair with /blog/how-to-get-rid-of-drain-flies-canada: written fresh from US sources (extension pages, EPA), no Canadian products or rules; add the pair to REGIONAL_PAIRS at release. Sources: University of Arkansas, UC IPM, University of Kentucky, Virginia Cooperative Extension ENTO-414, Alabama Cooperative Extension, Penn State, Purdue. One generic pick at most; no quote prompt.

pages.scope: Paper wasps (Polistes) for US and Canadian readers, identification first. The quick answer: slender wasps that let their long hind legs dangle in flight, brown, reddish or black-and-yellow by species, that build a single open comb of paper cells hanging from one stalk with no outer cover (the "umbrella" nest under eaves, porch ceilings, railings, shutters and play sets); less defensive than yellowjackets but they sting to defend the nest, at the sources' strength. The species, each with a photo where the ledger has one: the European paper wasp (Polistes dominula, black and yellow, often taken for a yellowjacket), the dark paper wasp (P. fuscatus), and red and other regional paper wasps only as sources list them. A quick-ID table under the quick answer (paper wasp, yellowjacket, bald-faced hornet, European hornet, mud dauber): color, body and waist, legs in flight, nest type and place, how defensive, sting. The nest through the year (started by one queen in spring, largest in late summer, abandoned in fall and not reused, as sources say) and why a nest by a door is a problem while one on a far corner can often be left (they hunt caterpillars: their value as predators at the sources' strength). The sting: what it does, first aid and when to get emergency care (an allergic reaction, many stings), from CDC/NIOSH, the American Academy of Dermatology or Mayo Clinic; link bee-sting-vs-wasp-sting once live. Removing a nest: when to leave it, when and how to remove it only as extension sources describe (after dark or early morning, protective clothing, a product labeled for wasps: the label is the law; never a homemade spray, fire or water), and when to call a professional (a nest out of reach, anyone allergic). Cards: yellowjacket (yellow-jackets, no link until live), mud dauber (mud-daubers, same release), bald-faced hornet (bald-faced-hornets), European hornet (european-hornets). Sources: Penn State Extension, Clemson HGIC, University of Kentucky, UC IPM, Texas A&M AgriLife, Missouri Department of Conservation, CDC/NIOSH (insects). No product names beyond the one generic pick; no quote prompt.

pages.scope: Assassin bugs (family Reduviidae) for US and Canadian readers, the wheel bug first because it is the one people find and photograph most (the cog-wheel crest on its back), identification first. The quick answer: predatory true bugs with a narrow head, a stout curved beak folded under it and long legs; most live outdoors on plants hunting other insects; the bite of a wheel bug or other assassin bug is very painful if one is handled, but they do not seek people out, at the sources' strength; kissing bugs are a separate, blood-feeding group in the same family (one short section that links /blog/kissing-bug-look-alikes, which keeps the vs searches). The species, each with a photo where the ledger has one: the wheel bug (Arilus cristatus) adult and its bright red-and-black nymphs, the milkweed assassin bug (Zelus longipes), the masked hunter (Reduvius personatus, the one that comes indoors, its nymphs camouflaged in dust and lint) and others only where a source and a photo exist. A quick-ID table under the quick answer (wheel bug, milkweed assassin bug, masked hunter, kissing bug, leaf-footed bug, western conifer seed bug): size, color and shape, beak, where found, bites or not. The bite: what it feels like and what to do, from extension and medical sources at their strength, never "dangerous" beyond what they say; Chagas disease only as CDC states which bugs carry the parasite (CDC's look-alike page names the wheel bug among bugs that do not), linking kissing-bugs and chagas-disease once live. Their value as garden predators. What to do: leave it, or move it with a container, never with bare hands. Cards: kissing bug (/blog/kissing-bug-look-alikes), leaf-footed bug (leaf-footed-bugs, no link until live), western conifer seed bug (western-conifer-seed-bugs, no link until live), boxelder bug (/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-boxelder-bugs). pages.scope: Booklice (psocids; indoors mostly Liposcelis) for US and Canadian readers who find tiny, pale, soft bugs on a windowsill, in a box of old books or papers, on cereal or flour packages, or in a new or damp house. The quick answer: tiny (sizes only from sources), wingless, grayish to translucent, quick-moving, with a large head; not true lice; they do not bite people or pets, and they feed on microscopic mold, so they are a sign of high humidity (each at the sources' strength). The common kinds, briefly (booklice indoors; winged barklice outdoors and on houseplants), with photos at a printed scale. Where they turn up and why: books and papers, wallpaper paste, stored food and pantry packages, new homes with damp plaster or drywall, basements, after a leak (as sources say). "Booklice in bed" and "booklice vs bed bugs": booklice do not feed on blood; how to tell them from bed bug nymphs, linking /blog/bugs-that-look-like-bed-bugs. Getting rid of them, humidity first, in order: dehumidify, ventilate, fix leaks, dry or discard moldy items, clean shelves, throw out infested food; insecticides only as sources say (they describe them as rarely needed). pages.scope: Mud daubers for US and Canadian readers, identification first: the solitary wasps that build nests of mud on walls, eaves, garages, sheds, porch ceilings and attics. The quick answer: a long, thread-thin waist; three common kinds, each with its nest: the black-and-yellow mud dauber (Sceliphron caementarium) and its lumpy clusters of cells, the organ-pipe mud dauber (Trypoxylon politum) and its long parallel tubes, and the blue mud dauber (Chalybion californicum), which reuses other daubers' nests; they rarely sting people, at the sources' strength, and they stock each cell with paralyzed spiders (black widows among them only where a source says so). "Dirt dauber" as a regional name. A quick-ID table under the quick answer (mud dauber, paper wasp, yellowjacket, cicada killer, and a potter wasp only if a source and a photo exist): waist, color, nest, behavior, sting. Reading a nest: active or old (round exit holes mean the adults have left, as sources say) and what is inside. When to remove nests and how (scrape off old nests; why sprays are rarely needed), only as extension sources put it. The sting and when to get care, at CDC/NIOSH or extension strength. Cards: paper wasp (paper-wasps, same release), yellowjacket (yellow-jackets, no link until live), cicada killer (cicada-killers, no link until live). Sources: Penn State Extension, University of Kentucky, Missouri Department of Conservation, Texas A&M AgriLife, UF/IFAS Featured Creatures, Clemson HGIC, NC State Extension. No quote prompt.

pages.scope: Roly polies for US and Canadian readers: the pill bug (Armadillidium vulgare), which rolls into a ball, and the sow bug (Porcellio), which cannot and has two short tail-like appendages; identification first. The quick answer: not insects but land crustaceans (isopods) that breathe with gills and need damp places; harmless to people, pets and the house; they wander in from mulch and leaf litter and usually die indoors because the air is too dry (each as sources say). Pill bug or sow bug, with photos, and the look-alikes in a quick-ID table under the quick answer (pill bug, sow bug, millipede, springtail, house centipede): legs, body shape, rolls up or not, where found, harmless or not. Babies (the female carries eggs and young in a pouch, only as sources say) and what they eat (decaying plant matter; when they nibble seedlings, ripening strawberries and other soft plant parts, at the sources' strength). Why they come indoors (damp basements and crawl spaces, door thresholds, after heavy rain, in fall) and what fixes it, moisture and habitat first, in order: dry the basement, pull mulch and leaf litter back from the foundation, seal gaps and add door sweeps, sweep or vacuum up the ones inside; insecticides only as extension sources put them (rarely needed indoors; any outdoor perimeter treatment only per the label). "Potato bug" as a regional name in one line that links jerusalem-crickets. The pet and terrarium searches (isopods for sale or for terrariums) are not targeted. Cards: millipede (/blog/millipedes), house centipede (/blog/house-centipedes), springtail (/blog/springtails), woodlouse spider (woodlouse-spiders, no link until live). Sources: University of Kentucky, Penn State Extension, UC IPM (sowbugs and pillbugs), Missouri Department of Conservation, Colorado State Extension, Clemson HGIC. No quote prompt.

Needed, none on record: a sow bug (Porcellio), a pill bug rolled into a ball, roly polies where people find them (a basement floor, a door threshold, under a flowerpot or in mulch; at least two), seedling or strawberry damage, a female with young.

pages.scope: Springtails (Collembola) for US readers who find tiny jumping bugs indoors, identification first. The quick answer: tiny (sizes only from sources, inches first), soft-bodied and wingless, white, gray, black or banded, and they flip into the air with a forked, tail-like spring folded under the body; they need moisture and are a sign of it, and they do not bite people or damage the house (Colorado State, UMN, Penn State, UC IPM, whichever say so). The two body shapes people see (long-bodied and round, globular springtails) with photos at a printed scale. Where they turn up and why: tubs, sinks and shower drains, damp basements and window sills, wet potting soil after watering, pool water, and outdoors in mulch and leaf litter, sometimes in large numbers by foundations (each only as a source says); snow fleas, the springtails that dot late-winter snow, in one short section (a winter search). "Baby springtails": young springtails look like small adults (no larval stage), only as a source says. "Springtail or flea?" in one short section that links /blog/bugs-that-look-like-fleas, which keeps "springtails vs fleas"; the tiny-black-bug and houseplant searches stay with /blog/tiny-black-bugs and /blog/houseplant-bugs (link both). How to get rid of springtails, moisture first, in order: fix leaks and drips, ventilate the bathroom, run a dehumidifier, let houseplant soil dry between waterings, pull mulch and leaf litter back from the foundation, seal gaps, vacuum the ones indoors (Colorado State, UMN); insecticides only at the sources' strength (Colorado State advises avoiding them indoors where possible; UMN says there are no pesticides for springtails in houseplants), never a home-remedy spray. Quick-ID table: the springtail and its look-alikes (flea, booklouse, mite, fungus gnat larva in soil), one row each: size, color, how it moves, where you find it, bites or not. Cards: flea (/blog/bugs-that-look-like-fleas), booklouse (no link: /blog/booklice is slated for replacement), silverfish (/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-silverfish), fungus gnat (/learn/how-to-get-rid-of-fungus-gnats). Sources: Colorado State Extension, UMN Extension, Penn State Extension, UC IPM, and a state extension page for snow fleas. No product advice beyond the one generic pick; no quote prompt (a traffic page).

pages.scope: The insect itself, by photo, for US readers: workers (pale, soft, ant-sized; the ones found in damaged wood), soldiers (larger tan or brown heads with jaws) and winged swarmers (dark bodies, two pairs of equal-length wings, straight antennae, a thick waist), with sizes only from sources; "white ants" and "baby termites" answered. The main US groups and how to tell them apart: eastern and other subterranean termites (Reticulitermes), the Formosan subterranean termite (Coptotermes formosanus) and drywood termites, with where each lives as sources map it and the sign that goes with each (pellets: /blog/termite-droppings; mud tubes and damage: /blog/termite-damage). Flying termites: when and where swarms appear (spring for most subterranean termites; other seasons and times for Formosan and drywood termites, at the sources' strength), what a swarm indoors means, and shed wings on windowsills. A quick-ID table under the quick answer (termite worker, termite swarmer, flying ant, carpenter ant, freshly molted white cockroach): color, waist, antennae, wings, where found. "Bugs that look like termites" as look-alike cards: flying ant (/blog/flying-ants-vs-termites, which keeps the comparison and "termites vs ants"), carpenter ant (/blog/do-carpenter-ants-bite), white cockroach (/blog/white-cockroach), termite droppings (/blog/termite-droppings). What to do: an inspection by a licensed professional when there are signs, at the sources' strength; no treatment claims or product names. Written now (pulled forward from February) so it is indexed and aged before the March-May swarm season. Sources: USDA Forest Service and ARS, UF/IFAS (Formosan and drywood termites), Texas A&M AgriLife, Clemson HGIC, Purdue, University of Kentucky, NC State Extension, EPA (termites). No quote prompt.

pages.scope: For the reader with itchy bites who has looked and found no bed bugs. First, whether it can still be bed bugs (they hide in seams and cracks by day, early infestations are small, and reactions vary and can take days to show: CDC, AAD, EPA), with how to check properly (/blog/signs-of-bed-bugs-checklist; interceptor traps). Then what else bites at night or indoors, each with a bite photo, the pattern, where on the body and the clue that points to it: fleas (ankles and lower legs; pets or wildlife), mosquitoes, bird and rodent mites (after a nest is removed or a rodent dies), bat and swallow bugs, chiggers and no-see-ums picked up outdoors, and spiders (rarely); then what is not a bite at all (scabies, carpet beetle larval hairs, skin conditions, irritants such as fiberglass, dry skin: CDC and UC IPM's itching guide). Get a specimen identified (a county extension office) before treating, why spraying for an unidentified biter does not help, and when to see a doctor (CDC, AAD, Mayo Clinic or Cleveland Clinic at their strength). Never diagnose: bites alone rarely name the biter, and CDC says bites cannot confirm bed bugs. Link /learn/bug-bites and /tools/bug-bite-identifier for the general "what bit me" search; the "invisible bugs biting me" searches stay with /blog/no-see-um-bites.

pages.scope: Supella longipalpa for US readers, identification first: a small roach about 1/2 inch long (UC IPM, Penn State, UF; up to 5/8 inch per Texas A&M and Clemson: give the range) with two light bands across the wings and abdomen (UC IPM), males golden tan with wings that cover the abdomen, females darker and broader with shorter wings (UC IPM, UF, Texas A&M); on adult males the wings can hide the bands (Clemson). Then the "light colored cockroach" question as a sorter, with a quick-ID table (one row per light-colored roach) and look-alike cards: brown-banded (bands across the body, found away from the kitchen), German (two dark stripes behind the head, kitchens and bathrooms; /blog/german-cockroaches), the Asian cockroach (looks like a German but flies to lights; /blog/can-cockroaches-fly) and a just-molted roach of any species (white, darkening within hours, per UC IPM; /blog/white-cockroach); "brown banded cockroach vs german cockroach" gets its own h2. Where it lives, the best tell after the bands: warm (about 80°F, UC IPM), dry, dim spots nearer the ceiling than the floor and away from water (Penn State, Texas A&M): upper walls, cabinets and closets, behind picture frames, under and inside furniture, in and near electronics and appliances (UC IPM, Penn State, Clemson), not the kitchen-and-sink spots of the German cockroach; UC IPM's "about 1% of indoor infestations" is a California figure, so say so. Egg cases glued in clusters under furniture and drawers, on ceilings and in closets, about 1/4 inch (UC IPM, Clemson), a habit that spreads the species with furniture (Ebeling, as /blog/cockroach-eggs cites him): one short section that links /blog/cockroach-eggs. Nymphs, signs and how they get in get a short section each, linking /blog/what-do-baby-cockroaches-look-like (which keeps the "baby" searches), /blog/signs-of-cockroaches and /blog/where-do-cockroaches-come-from. Whether it flies is one FAQ that links /blog/can-cockroaches-fly, at the sources' strength (males only: sometimes when disturbed, especially above 85°F, per UC IPM; readily, per Penn State). Health at the sources' strength (allergens and asthma from EPA; carried bacteria only as Penn State puts it). Control goes to /blog/how-to-get-rid-of-cockroaches (UC IPM says baits work less well on this species; no product advice here). pages.scope: The page for the reader who hears something in the wall, identification first: what is in the wall, by sound, time and sign. Scratching, scurrying and squeaking at night (mice: Nebraska); rats, mainly roof rats, which nest in attics and wall voids (UC IPM); noise by day from gray squirrels and at night from flying squirrels (as /blog/animals-in-attic sorts them, UGA); squeaking and chattering around dusk (bats: USFWS); a faint rustling (carpenter ants: UC IPM); and the insects that winter in wall voids and wander out on warm days (/blog/bugs-in-house-in-winter). Quick-ID table, one row per suspect: what you hear, when, the droppings, the other sign. For each suspect a photo, the sign that confirms it (droppings and their size, a musky smell, gnaw marks, dark rub marks at holes and along pipes, shredded nesting material; NPS Conserve O Gram 3/12 shows mouse signs) and a link (/blog/rat-vs-mouse, /blog/roof-rat-vs-norway-rat, /blog/animals-in-attic, /blog/bat-poop, /blog/mouse-poop, /blog/mouse-urine). Then how mice get into and travel through walls (openings of 1/4 inch, along pipes, wires and sill plates; climbing goes to /blog/can-mice-climb-walls) and how to get them out without sealing them in: snap traps where they leave the wall (behind the stove and refrigerator, under sinks, where pipes enter, above drop ceilings: CDC, Nebraska; trap types go to /blog/mice-traps), traps set and working before the last holes are closed and a week with no catches before calling it done (CDC, consistent with /blog/fall-mouse-proofing-checklist and /blog/steel-wool-for-mice), and why poison and ultrasonic devices are a poor fit for wall voids (UC IPM, Cornell, Nebraska; /blog/mice-poison). A dead mouse in the wall: why it happens, how long the smell lasts (Cornell: days for a mouse), when opening the wall is worth it; finding and removing the carcass stays on /blog/mice-removal. When to call a pro: /blog/mice-exterminator. Health only from CDC at its strength (never sweep or vacuum droppings or nests; hantavirus and which mice carry it: /blog/deer-mice). Sources: CDC rodent control (seal up, trap up, clean up), EPA, Nebraska Extension G1105, UC IPM Pest Notes (house mouse, rats, carpenter ants), Cornell, Penn State, Purdue, NPS Conserve O Gram 3/12, the USFWS bat manual, UGA. No product advice; no quote prompt (a traffic page; BuzzSkito does not treat rodents).

pages.scope: The flea dirt page, identification first: what flea dirt is (the digested blood adult fleas excrete as they feed: Ohio State, Texas A&M, the University of Florida's cat flea profile, Penn State's cat flea fact sheet), what it looks like at life size and magnified (black to reddish-black specks like ground pepper, comma-shaped up close: the University of Minnesota's veterinary diagnostics textbook, the Merck Veterinary Manual; a size only if a source gives one), and the wet paper towel test as the centerpiece, step by step: comb the pet over white paper, a white sink or a pillowcase, put the specks on a damp white paper towel, and flea dirt dissolves into reddish-brown smears where ordinary dirt does not (Ohio State, Minnesota, Merck, Cornell Feline Health Center). Where to look: on a dog, the neck, shoulder blades and base of the tail, belly and groin (Ohio State, Minnesota, Merck); on a cat, the back of the neck, the top of the tail head, belly and back (Cornell Feline Health Center); with a fine-toothed flea comb; then pet bedding, resting spots, beds and carpet, and for cats shelves and tabletops (Ohio State). A photo strip and quick-ID table, flea dirt vs ordinary dirt vs flea eggs vs dandruff, and look-alike cards (flea eggs; bed bug poop, which also runs red but stains mattress seams; cockroach specks). What finding it means: adult fleas are feeding on the animal now, even when none is seen (Merck: dogs very allergic to flea saliva may be almost free of fleas because they groom so much), and larvae develop where flea dirt collects because they feed on it (only as UF, UC IPM and Penn State put it); flea dirt but no fleas; flea dirt in a bed. Whether it is harmful, at the sources' strength: CDC's flea-borne typhus page (infected flea dirt rubbed into bites or other wounds; murine-typhus once live) and cat-scratch disease page (scratches contaminated with flea feces), anemia in heavily infested kittens and puppies (Cornell, Merck), tapeworm (Texas A&M, Cornell). What to do: treat every pet with a product a veterinarian recommends, never a dog product on a cat (Cornell; CDC: never permethrin on cats), wash pet bedding hot and vacuum often (UC IPM), then /blog/how-to-get-rid-of-fleas for the full plan; no product advice here. Not a second eggs page: eggs, larvae and cocoons stay with /blog/flea-eggs (one short section and a link), the adult flea with /blog/what-do-fleas-look-like. Sources: CDC (About Fleas, Getting Rid of Fleas, flea-borne typhus, cat-scratch disease), UC IPM Pest Notes: Fleas, Texas A&M AgriLife Managing Fleas, Ohio State HYG-2081, Penn State Extension Cat Fleas, UF/IFAS Featured Creatures cat flea (EENY-011), the Minnesota textbook, Merck, Cornell Feline Health Center (Fleas: A Source of Torment for Your Cat), AVMA (External parasites).

pages.scope: For US travelers, the hotel check first, in the order to do it. Keep luggage off the floor and off the bed until the check is done, on a luggage rack, table or other hard surface (University of Kentucky ENTFACT-636; EPA's Protecting Your Home from Bed Bugs says to inspect the luggage rack). Check the bed from the pillow end with a flashlight: sheets and pillows back, mattress seams, piping and tags, and the box spring where it can be seen (Kentucky); the headboard edges and the gap behind it, a frequent hiding place in hotel rooms, without taking it down (Kentucky warns untrained people not to); then the nightstand, upholstered chairs and the luggage rack straps. What the signs look like in a hotel bed (live bugs, ink-dot fecal spots, shed skins, eggs), with photos at life size, linking /blog/signs-of-bed-bugs-checklist, /blog/bed-bug-poop and /blog/what-do-bed-bugs-look-like; why a clean check is not proof (Virginia Tech: in a new infestation, a hotel room for example, evidence can be very hard to find). If you find them: tell the front desk, ask for a room in a different part of the hotel because infestations sometimes extend to nearby units (Kentucky), photograph the evidence and keep luggage closed; who must act is set by states and cities, not EPA (EPA's Bed Bug Laws and Regulations page: 21 states with some law or regulation, focused mostly on hotels and landlords), stated at that strength, no legal advice. Bites during or after a trip: marks can take as long as 14 days to show and bites alone do not confirm bed bugs (CDC), and bites noticed after getting home do not mean the home is infested (Virginia Tech); link /blog/bed-bug-bites and /blog/bed-bug-bites-but-no-bed-bugs. Coming home: unpack away from the bedroom, put clothing straight into the washer or dryer (heat settings only as a source gives them), heat-treat or isolate a suitcase you are worried about (Kentucky: a hot car in summer; Rutgers: a portable heating box), why Kentucky rates inspecting or vacuuming a suitcase as less useful, how to watch for bed bugs at home afterwards (interceptors under the bed legs; /blog/signs-of-bed-bugs-checklist) and what to do if they came home (/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-bed-bugs). For perspective, Kentucky says most hotel infestations are limited to a few rooms. A where-to-check table (spot, what to look for, how to check it) and look-alike cards (bat bug, carpet beetle larva, cockroach nymph, spider beetle; /blog/bugs-that-look-like-bed-bugs). Hiding places in general go to /blog/where-do-bed-bugs-hide. Sources: EPA (How to Find Bed Bugs; Protecting Your Home from Bed Bugs; Bed Bug Laws and Regulations), CDC, University of Kentucky ENTFACT-636, Virginia Tech, Rutgers and the Indiana Department of Health, as already cited on /blog/where-do-bed-bugs-hide and /learn/bed-bugs. Never name a hotel, chain, booking or registry site; no spray or product advice beyond the one generic pick; no quote prompt (a traffic page; BuzzSkito does not treat bed bugs).

pages.scope: The life stage that does the damage, for US and Canadian readers who find a tiny, hairy "worm" on a carpet edge, in a closet, a drawer, a bed or a windowsill; identification first. The quick answer: carpet beetle larvae are small, bristly, brown-banded or golden-brown and slow-moving, often found with their shed skins; they eat wool, fur, feathers, silk, leather, dead insects and lint, not synthetic fabric alone (UC IPM), while adults feed on pollen outdoors (each at the sources' strength). The common kinds, each with a photo and its tell: the varied carpet beetle larva (Anthrenus verbasci: banded, with tufts of long hairs at the tail end), the black carpet beetle larva (Attagenus: longer, carrot-shaped, golden-brown, with a long tail tuft) and the furniture carpet beetle larva only where a source describes it; size and how long they stay larvae only from sources. Where they hide and why: under furniture and along baseboards, in closets with wool or stored clothes, in pet hair and lint, near bird nests or dead insects in attics and on windowsills, and in beds and mattresses (sources differ: say what each says; "carpet beetle larvae in bed"). A quick-ID table under the quick answer (carpet beetle larva, clothes moth larva, bed bug nymph, flea larva, an outdoor woolly bear caterpillar): size, shape, hairs, where found, damage. "Carpet weevils" answered in one line (a name people use for carpet beetles). Shed skins and the damage pattern in one short section each that link /blog/signs-of-carpet-beetles. Do they bite or cause a rash: the larvae do not bite; their hairs can irritate some people's skin, at the sources' strength, linking carpet-beetle-rash once live. What to do first (find the food source, vacuum, wash or freeze infested items, as sources say) in a short section that links /blog/how-to-get-rid-of-carpet-beetles, which keeps every control search. Cards: clothes moth larva (/blog/moths-in-house), bed bug look-alikes (/blog/bugs-that-look-like-bed-bugs), flea larva (/blog/flea-eggs), signs of carpet beetles (/blog/signs-of-carpet-beetles). Sources: UC IPM, University of Kentucky, NC State Extension, Penn State Extension, Ohio State, Colorado State, UMN Extension, and CDC's Emerging Infectious Diseases report on carpet beetle dermatitis only at its strength. No quote prompt.

pages.scope: Weevils for US and Canadian readers, the two places people find them first: in stored grain at home, and wandering indoors from outside. The quick answer: weevils are small beetles with a long snout; in the pantry, the rice, granary and maize weevils (Sitophilus) breed inside whole kernels (rice, wheat, corn, popcorn and other whole grains or seeds, as sources list them), not in flour, so the bugs in flour are usually flour beetles (link /blog/pantry-pests); outdoors, root weevils (black vine and strawberry root weevils) come indoors in late summer and fall, and acorn and nut weevil larvae crawl out of stored acorns and nuts, each as sources say; weevils do not bite people or pets and do not damage the house. Identification, each with a photo: the rice weevil (four pale spots on the wing covers), the granary weevil (no spots; it cannot fly) and the maize weevil only as sources separate it; bean and pea weevils (seed beetles) in dried beans in one short line; root weevils indoors. Where they came from: infested grain from the store or a bulk bin, a forgotten bag, bird seed or pet food (as sources say). Getting rid of pantry weevils, in order: find and discard every infested package, check whole grains, dried beans, bird seed and pet food, vacuum and wipe shelves, freeze or heat new grain only with the times and temperatures a source gives, store food in sealed containers; why sprays are not used on food shelves (the label is the law). pages.scope: The vocabulary question first, then the animal people actually meet. The quick answer: in the US and Canada "possum" is the everyday name for the Virginia opossum (Didelphis virginiana), the only marsupial north of Mexico; the possums of Australia and New Guinea are a different group of marsupials that share the name (each point only as a museum, a state wildlife agency or a university says it). A quick-ID table under the quick answer: Virginia opossum vs Australian common brushtail possum (and a ringtail possum only if a source and a photo exist): where it lives, size, fur, face, tail, feet, how it defends itself, what it eats; add a row for the raccoon people mistake an opossum for at night. Then the North American opossum: what it looks like (sizes from a state agency or university), range (north into southern Canada, as sources say), the prehensile tail and the thumb on the hind foot, playing dead (what it is, at the sources' strength), babies (pouch, then riding on the mother), lifespan, are opossums dangerous (bites when cornered; rabies only at CDC's or a state health department's strength, never "immune to rabies"; any other disease only if a primary source names it), the tick-eating claim in one or two sentences linking /blog/do-chickens-eat-ticks, diet in one line linking /blog/what-eats-ticks-and-mosquitoes, an opossum in the yard, under a deck, in a garage or attic (what state wildlife agencies advise: remove pet food and fallen fruit, secure trash, close gaps once it has left; trapping and relocation only as the state agency says, noting that rules differ by state; link /blog/animals-in-attic), and droppings in one line linking /blog/animal-droppings. Cards: raccoon (/blog/raccoon-poop), rat (/blog/rat-vs-mouse), opossum droppings (/blog/animal-droppings). Sources: the Smithsonian's National Zoo or NMNH, state wildlife agencies (Missouri Department of Conservation, Pennsylvania Game Commission, NY DEC, Texas Parks and Wildlife), the Australian Museum or an Australian state agency for the possums, CDC (rabies), ICWDM. No quote prompt; no product advice beyond the one generic pick.

pages.scope: US edition of /blog/how-to-get-rid-of-voles-canada, written fresh for US readers (US species, ranges and extension sources; no Canadian retail or regulators). The animal first: what a vole looks like (a small, stocky rodent with a blunt face, small eyes, ears half-hidden in fur and a short tail; sizes only from sources) and the US voles people meet: meadow, prairie and pine (woodland) voles in the East and Midwest, the California and montane voles in the West, each only where a source covers it. A quick-ID table under the quick answer: vole, house mouse, deer mouse, shrew, mole: snout, eyes and ears, tail, fur, food, signs (linking /blog/field-mice, /blog/shrews, /blog/holes-in-yard). Signs and damage: surface runways in grass (most visible at snowmelt), small burrow openings without mounds (sizes as sources give them), gnawed bark and roots at the base of trees and shrubs, bulbs and root crops eaten from below; vole or mole damage in one paragraph linking /blog/holes-in-yard (which keeps "mole vs vole"). When voles are worst (population cycles, winter damage under snow, as sources say). How to get rid of voles: cut cover (mow, pull mulch and weeds back from trunks), 1/4-inch hardware cloth cylinders around trunks, snap traps set across runways, repellents and baits only at extension and label strength (rodenticides: the label is the law, no poison recipes), and what does not work only where a source says so. Are voles dangerous (bites when handled; disease only at CDC's or a state health department's strength). Cards: field mouse (/blog/field-mice), shrew (/blog/shrews), mole (/blog/holes-in-yard), house mouse (/blog/types-of-mice). Sources: UC IPM Pest Notes: Voles, ICWDM, Penn State, University of Minnesota, NC State or Cornell extension, Missouri Department of Conservation. No quote prompt.

method: Inventory read on 2026-10-14: every folder in app/blog (434), content/guides (86 guides), app/learn, app/tools, the root service and city routes, data/us-pages/routes.json and plan.json, data/god-build/plan.src.json (120 scheduled pages), next.config.mjs redirects. The build script rejects any slug that exists, is planned or scheduled, is a redirect source, carries a geo token, or whose meta title is over 48 characters; every collision path must exist.

Collisions were judged by meaning, not slug: each page lists the existing pages that answer the same or an overlapping question, what they rank for (Search Console), and how the two are kept apart (a regional pair with hreflang, a section trimmed to a summary plus a link, or a head term left with the existing page).

Demand: Search Console query data for the 90 days to 2026-10-12 (scratchpad growth/gsc_growth.json, single-dimension query pulls, all countries and US). Each page carries the regex used, the totals, its top queries and the pages Google showed for them (from the sampled page x query pull; use only for "which page", not totals).

Google autocomplete (suggestqueries, hl=en, gl=us) was fetched for each topic as evidence that demand exists. It gives no volume, and the requests left from an Ontario IP, so some suggestions are Canadian (e.g. "black widow spider toronto").

Ahrefs was not used for new volumes: the API key had 59 of 100,000 units left (resets 2026-10-26), and the operating rules say Ahrefs volume is unreliable for Canadian long-tail terms. The two October Ahrefs files were checked for every keyword; none of the new primaries is in them.

priorityDefinition.1: Search Console already shows demand (roughly 300+ impressions in 90 days) that lands on a page that does not answer it or ranks worse than 8; or a US edition of a Canadian page where Search Console shows the topic's demand landing on the Canadian page (no-see-ums: 2,226 US impressions; deer fly vs horse fly: 1,469 US; the tick species pages: 55-229 US on pages ranked 9-14) while the US topic is clearly searched; and the page can carry something competitors lack (CDC county maps, real photos).
priorityDefinition.2: Demand confirmed by autocomplete depth or by adjacent Search Console data, a clear entity or comparison in a cluster where bite and identification pages already perform, assets available or obtainable.
priorityDefinition.3: Completes a cluster or covers a real but small topic; build after priority 1 and 2 have been indexed. Gated pages wait for their stated condition.

notes.honestEarnings: The skill's measured economics apply: most new pages join the long tail. For scale, the strongest existing bite page (/blog/no-see-um-bites) took 880 clicks in 90 days; at the $30 RPM used in the growth plan that is roughly $10-12 a month. Most pages here will earn far less; the case for the list is cumulative ad traffic on pages that match how this site already ranks (identification, bites, comparisons) and the internal links that lift the existing bite pages, not per-page income. Re-check with Search Console 60-90 days after each wave and stop a family that returns nothing.

implementation: GuideCluster in lib/guides.ts allows only bed-bugs, ants, mice, cockroaches, mosquitoes, ticks, pest-control and garden. Pages in the new clusters (spiders, stinging-insects, flies, mites, fleas, household, kissing-bugs, scorpions, bites) are given guideCluster "pest-control" so they render today, but "Keep reading" cards and recirculation would then mix them with pest-control articles. Extending GuideCluster (plus CLUSTER_LABEL, CLUSTER_PILLAR and the FALLBACK map in scripts/build-article-index.mjs) before the first of these releases is the cleaner route.

Audience maps to the validator: "us" = no audience field (US English, Fahrenheit, inches); "ca" = audience "ca" with locale en-CA; "na" = audience "na" (US English with both units and both countries' regulators allowed).

Photos: photos.json covers ticks and mosquitoes only, so tick and mosquito pages are first in the release order. The validator refuses any figure not recorded there. Spiders, mites, fleas, bed bugs, midges and bites are being sourced; stinging insects, flies, kissing bugs, scorpions, household and garden pests still need sourcing (CDC PHIL and USDA/USGS images are public domain, the USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab covers bees and wasps; Bugwood images are mostly CC BY-NC and are not allowed). parent null (natural-mosquito-repellent, permethrin-for-clothing) means the guide falls back to its cluster pillar (CLUSTER_PILLAR in lib/guides.ts).

Release order puts every new hub in the same or an earlier wave than its spokes; the release script needs a live hub before a spoke goes out, so if both fall on one Monday release the hub first or move it a week earlier.

Tools (/tools/what-bit-me, /tools/tick-identifier) are not on the Mediavine allow-list; adding them is the owner's call. They follow the /tools/what-bug-is-this pattern (real photos only, GA4 quiz events).

To schedule a page: copy its fields into data/god-build/extra-pages.json (slug, section, cluster -> use guideCluster until the type is extended, keyword, alsoTargets, h1Hint = title, scope, flags, minWords, parent, mustLink, audience when not "us"), then run node scripts/god-build-plan.mjs and node scripts/us-pages-plan.mjs.
